title: Agentic AI Build Week Recap
content:
FCAJ x Agentic AI Build Week Show Up. Build. Pitch. WIN! Below is the recap by team based on the transcript of the FCAJ x Agentic AI Build Week Show Up. Build. Pitch. WIN! event. The content focuses on 4 perspectives:
Key highlight Core idea Lessons learned Feelings & feedback on the presentation Teams: Team 1 - KFC Ordering Agent (First Prize) Team Signal Scout - Strategic Intelligence Platform (Second Prize) Team BL - AI Solution Architect Assistant Summary of Key Takeaways from All 3 Teams Topic Lessons Learned Problem First Start with pain points instead of technology Business Always answer: who will use it? why do they need it? MVP A working demo is more important than complete features Storytelling Use case studies to guide the narrative Architecture Design modular architecture for scalability Cost Knowing how to estimate AWS costs creates a competitive advantage Teamwork Debate but align on the direction together Execution A good idea without implementation is practically meaningless Pitching Judges care more about how problems are solved than the number of AWS services used Networking Hackathons are not just for competing, but for building relations & learning General Feelings about the Presentations What I appreciated most was that the teams did not just present “what we built”, but also shared “how we thought”. The key messages that appeared throughout:
Always start with a real problem rather than the technology. In hackathons, execution and demo are more critical than an overly ambitious architecture. Business mindset and storytelling can decide the outcome as much as programming skills. Effective teamwork requires knowing how to debate, but also how to compromise and execute together. These lessons are valuable not just for hackathons but also for building real-world products later on.

title: Team 1 - KFC Ordering Agent
content:
Team 1 (First Prize AWS Track) Project: AI Conversational Ordering Agent for KFC ⭐ Key highlight Selected a highly practical problem: ordering food directly within a chat application instead of forcing users to install a dedicated app. Did not just jump into the solution, but started with a case study of McDonald’s failed AI Drive-through, helping the audience understand the pain point clearly beforehand. The architecture was designed as multi-channel, easily extensible to other brands besides KFC. Provided calculations of AWS costs, latency, and scalability, not just a simple mockup demo. 💡 Idea Building an AI Agent that enables customers to:
Order KFC directly on Zalo/WhatsApp. No app download required. Natural language understanding (NLU). Automated memory of order history. Order verification step before submission to avoid hallucinations. Workflow:
Chat ↓ Intent Understanding ↓ Planning ↓ Tool Calling ↓ Menu ↓ Promotion ↓ Verify ↓ Order Additionally, a dashboard is provided for staff to monitor conversation logs if the AI encounters issues.
📚 Lessons Learned 1. Pitching should start with the Problem Do not open with architecture. Start with: “McDonald’s once failed because…” => the audience immediately grasps the pain point. This is an excellent storytelling technique.
2. Architecture should be modular They built:
Channel Adapter Agent Core Memory Tool Dashboard => Changing KFC to Jollibee later on only requires changing the connector. This represents a solid software architecture mindset.
3. Always include a Verify step They emphasized that AI is not always right. Thus, there is always:
Verify -> Customer confirms -> Submit This is a very effective way to reduce hallucinations.
4. Cost is also a part of the product They calculated infrastructure cost, latency, and Amazon Bedrock cost. This makes the project feel production-ready.
💬 Presentation Feelings This was the most balanced presentation between Business, Technical, Demo, and AWS. What I liked most was that they constantly referred back to “customer experience” instead of just boasting about how powerful the AI was. The project has high practical viability.

title: Team Signal Scout
content:
Team Signal Scout (Second Prize) Project: Multi-Agent Strategic Intelligence Platform ⭐ Key highlight The most outstanding aspect of this team was not their architecture, but their ideation process. They spent considerable time sharing how they identified the right pain points rather than which AWS services to use. This is a mindset highly worth adopting.
💡 Idea A Multi-Agent system that assists enterprises in:
Crawling competitor data. Aggregating business signals. Analyzing strategic moves. Predicting ROI if similar strategies are implemented. Workflow:
Competitor -> Financial reports / News / Organization -> AI Agent -> Business Recommendation Target customers: Strategy teams, Enterprises, Risk management. 📚 Lessons Learned 1. Technology cannot triumph over the Problem Perhaps the best quote of the day: “No matter how cool the technology is, it cannot exceed the boundaries of business requirements.” This is an aspect many students tend to overlook.
2. Concept is more important than complete code In a hackathon, you do not need 100% completion. What matters is identifying the right problem, defining the correct target customer, and having a working demo.
3. MVP > Perfect They emphasized that many teams fail due to scope creep, ending up with unfinished code and no demo. It is much better to have a 20% scope that runs than a 100% scope that does not.
4. Teamwork They shared honest stories about arguments, brainstorming sessions, and setting aside egos to align on a single direction. This is a common path for almost any hackathon team.
5. What do the Judges care about? An interesting insight: Judges asking many questions is not a bad sign; it means they are highly engaged. You should worry if they ask nothing at all.
💬 Presentation Feelings This was my favorite session regarding product and team mindset. It did not focus on bragging about technology but instead shared valuable battle-tested experiences on ideation, pitching, teamwork, MVP, and scope management. If you are preparing for a hackathon, this is a must-listen.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Here, you can freely share your personal opinions about your experience participating in the First Cloud AI Journey program. This will help the FCAJ team improve any shortcomings based on the following aspects:
Overall Evaluation 1. Working Environment
The working environment is very friendly and open. FCAJ members are always willing to help whenever I encounter difficulties, even outside working hours. The workspace is tidy and comfortable, helping me focus better. However, I think it would be nice to have more social gatherings or team bonding activities to strengthen relationships.
2. Support from Mentor / Team Admin
The mentor provides very detailed guidance, explains clearly when I don’t understand, and always encourages me to ask questions. The admin team supports administrative tasks, provides necessary documents, and creates favorable conditions for me to work effectively. I especially appreciate that the mentor allows me to try and solve problems myself instead of just giving the answer.
3. Relevance of Work to Academic Major
The tasks I was assigned align well with the knowledge I learned at university, while also introducing me to new areas I had never encountered before. This allowed me to both strengthen my foundational knowledge and gain practical skills.
4. Learning & Skill Development Opportunities
During the internship, I learned many new skills such as using project management tools, teamwork skills, and professional communication in a corporate environment. The mentor also shared valuable real-world experiences that helped me better plan my career path.
5. Company Culture & Team Spirit
The company culture is very positive: everyone respects each other, works seriously but still keeps things enjoyable. When there are urgent projects, everyone works together and supports one another regardless of their position. This made me feel like a real part of the team, even as an intern.
6. Internship Policies / Benefits
The company provides an internship allowance and offers flexible working hours when needed. In addition, having the opportunity to join internal training sessions is a big plus.

title: Team BL
content:
Team BL Project: AI Solution Architect Assistant ⭐ Key highlight They started from a practical workplace pain point: Customers often request architecture design, cost estimation, and deployment options in an extremely short timeframe. This is a very common challenge faced by Solution Architects (SA).
💡 Idea An AI system that takes natural language requirements and corporate policies as input, then automatically generates architecture diagrams, cost estimations, and Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) templates (Terraform / CloudFormation), and supports automated deployment.
Workflow:
Requirement -> AI -> Architecture / Cost / IaC (Terraform/CloudFormation) -> Deploy 📚 Lessons Learned 1. AI should aim to boost productivity AI does not replace SAs. Instead, it slashes prep time from 2 days to 30 minutes, allowing the Solution Architect to focus on reviews and optimization.
2. Context is king The team allowed uploading organizational policies, guidelines, and company standards. This ensures that the generated architecture aligns perfectly with corporate compliance.
3. End-to-end automation Instead of stopping at drawing diagrams or estimating costs, they pushed the solution further by generating IaC and enabling automated provisioning. This is a complete Agentic workflow.
💬 Presentation Feelings The idea is incredibly powerful, especially for anyone who has worked in cloud infrastructure or SA roles. The only minor drawback was that the transcript got cut off, so we did not see their full demo and final wrap-up. Nonetheless, their approach of “AI assisting SA” is highly distinct from the other two teams as it focuses on boosting engineers’ internal efficiency rather than end-user issues.
